📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

The Dane Steadman Interview: Hard Going and High Stakes in the Karakoram

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1384 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, there is much more to an expedition than summit or failure.
  • In a recent development, the one factor on the team’s side was the previous experience of Steadman and Cody Winckler.
  • Grant Stewart of Canada, the third member of the Sosbun Brakk team, is a skilled climber but was less familiar with the Karakoram.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, there is much more to an expedition than summit or failure. In this exclusive interview, American climber Dane Steadman explains why his recent upcoming route on Karakoram’s Sosbun Brakk (6,414m) “was much more difficult than the one on Yashkuk Sar, both on and off the mountain.” Strong words, considering that he and his partners were awarded a Piolet d’Or for Yashkuk Sar.

In a recent development, the one factor on the team’s side was the previous experience of Steadman and Cody Winckler. “It was our third trip, so we knew a lot more about climbing there,” Steadman said. Indeed, after Yashkuk Sar, Winckler and Steadman returned to Pakistan in 2025 and climbed two upcoming routes with Blake Berghoff.

Grant Stewart of Canada, the third member of the Sosbun Brakk team, is a skilled climber but was less familiar with the Karakoram. His most remarkable climbs had taken place in Alaska and at home in the Canadian Rockies.

Bivy in an ice cave. Photo Dane Steadman.

Comparing the two epic climbs, Steadman highlighted the differences.

“The trip to Yashkuk Sar went incredibly smoothly. Getting there and acclimatizing was great. We had an amazing weather window for the climb. Nothing on it was exceptionally hard, and we did it on the first try, and the descent went without a hitch,” he noted.

Recent findings suggest that he explained that the hardest parts of that 2024 first ascent were their lack of experience and the uncertainty that came with it. An unexpected mishap also occurred during the climb itself: a snow mushroom collapsed above them, forcing them to change their ascent route halfway up.

“On the other hand,” Steadman went on, “almost everything about the Sosbun Brakk trip was hard: lost bags, sickness acclimatizing, big storms beforehand and while on the mountain, hard climbing and route-finding, and a very difficult descent through terrible weather.”.

It has been revealed that the unclimbed north face of Sosbun Brakk. Photo: Dane Steadman.

According to recent reports, “[Overall,] on the Yashkuk trip, I think we felt for most of the time that we would be able to do it with only some moments of doubt here and there,” Steadman admitted. “On Sosbun, we thought much of the time that we wouldn’t be able to do it for all the reasons above. We were quite surprised [to succeed].”.

One unusual aspect of the Sosbun Brakk expedition was its dates. They went to Pakistan and climbed in early fall, two months later than the Karakoram’s typical July-August climbing season. Yet, Steadman states this was planned to account for the changing climate in the high ranges.

Sources indicate that approaching the face. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“First, while the Karakoram doesn’t receive as much of the Indian monsoon as the main Himalaya, it is still a monsoonal climate, and I think (and have heard from many locals now) that the weather tends to be much better in the fall than in the summer,” he explained.

Recent findings suggest that “Second, we were concerned about rockfall and generally unsafe conditions on the face, being relatively low and lacking in buttresses. We thought the colder temperatures would make things safer and increase the odds of finding good ice.

Sources indicate that “Third, Grant was able to get time off in October more easily than earlier in September. In a perfect world, we probably would have gone one to two weeks earlier, but we worked with what we had.”.

It has been revealed that asked about other expeditions planning to visit the Pakistani mountains in the future, Steadman suggests that October could be a good time for certain climbs, but that September is also great. “This year, the weather was much less stable in September-October than I’ve experienced on my previous trips. Things got much snowier than normal for that time of year, [according to locals], but I think the weather was still better than through most of the summer.”.

Sources indicate that the team planned a single alpine-style push in the purest style. However, when they started on the route, they encountered an impassable hanging serac. They had to retreat and decide whether to try a totally different line or go home.

The base camp crew. Photo: Dane Steadman.

The team decided to try a route to the right of the originally planned one. But how could they be sure they wouldn’t reach another dead end?

Steadman admitted it was difficult. “The line we ended up climbing was entirely hidden from view at our base camp and where we acclimatized,” he explained. “[It was] an east-facing gash on a north face, which we only saw from the northwest until we tried it. From all the views we had before the first attempt, the central line we first attempted appeared to be the only route that wouldn’t involve climbing huge walls of monolithic gneiss, as it followed ice streaks and sheets for a good amount of it, and only looked to have relatively short cruxes.

Sources indicate that at the base, they discovered that a tiny but menacing serac hung over the center of the wall, threatening the lower half. (The upper half appeared protected by an overhanging rock wall above it.).

“So we shifted to a different line to the left, which looked much harder but possible, and planned to rejoin our intended line at mid-height, under the protection of the overhangs.

That attempt didn’t so much dead-end as things compounded, forcing a retreat. “We were tired even on the approach from non-stop efforts to get there and acclimatize. We had some equipment challenges, were moving slowly, and most of all, the climbing was damn hard,” he mentioned.

In the end, they chose to rappel down after a two-hour-plus lead climb on a pitch that hadn’t looked hard from below. Dusk was approaching; there was no bivy spot in sight, and they were only 300m up the 1,800m wall.

“However, from our position on that attempt, we were able to see the right-trending, east-facing gash on the right side of the face, which was totally hidden by monolithic rock walls from all our previous vantage points,” he said. “So, after bailing, we felt like the central line would require fresh bodies, minds, and a huge weather window, but the right-hand line would be much more feasible.”.

Recent findings suggest that heading up. Photo: Dane Steadman.

The climbers rested for three days in base camp and then set off again. “We certainly felt that we could get shut down at any number of points, especially at the steep mushroom-choked chimney on the headwall below the junction with the northwest spur,” Steadman admitted. “But it seemed like there was a good chance we could do it, and, most importantly, we felt like we could bail from anywhere [if necessary].”.

The summit ridge of Sosbun Brakk after many tough decisions. Photo: Dane Steadman.

However, bailing would not be easy. “The lower part would involve rappelling off V-threads, he explained, and if they had to turn back below the headwall, they would need to rappel out right to an icefield.

Route topo: line of ascent in red, line of descent in yellow. Photo: Steadman/Stewart.

The trio summited on their fifth day on the wall, at 4 pm. Days were now short, and they still had a long, uncertain descent ahead. The descent began on the line of ascent, but eventually deviated to new terrain.

“We descended the upper half of our route, almost entirely rappelling down the northwest spur, with a little bit of downclimbing/traversing),” Steadman noted.

In a recent development, they then reached a point west of their ascent line, where the face was slightly smaller and more covered in permanent ice. “Then we rappelled straight down, diagonaling back left partway down to avoid some serac hazard.”.

It has been revealed that descending in worsening weather. Photo: Dane Steadman.

According to recent reports, dane Steadman and Cody Winckler of the U.S., together with Grant Stewart of Canada, completed the first ascent of the north face of Sosbun Brakk (6,414m) in Pakistan’s Karakoram last month. The peak had been climbed only once before, by a Japanese team in 1981, from a different, milder side. The new 1,800m route includes difficulties of M7, WI5.

#228550. Natural Wonders: Crowley Lake Columns

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1080 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Natural Wonders: Crowley Lake Columns

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1080 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that it is low tide on Crowley Lake in Mono County, California.
  • It has been revealed that crowley Lake is a man-made reservoir, administered by the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power.
  • It has been revealed that father Crowley made it his mission to bolster tourism in the area.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it is low tide on Crowley Lake in Mono County, California. The water is still, the trout abundant, and one or two kayakers paddle about, enjoying the lack of tourists. But as you walk along the shore, something out of place appears: spiral pillars and arches that seem left over from some ancient civilization.

It has been revealed that crowley Lake is a man-made reservoir, administered by the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power. It was named after an key figure in the community, affectionately known as the Desert Padre. This beloved Catholic priest worked tirelessly to help a community that experienced water shortages throughout the 1920s and 1930s. Water from the nearby Owen Valley was diverted to Los Angeles, leaving very little for local residents.

It has been revealed that father Crowley made it his mission to bolster tourism in the area. The publicity led authorities to help locals by drawing up looks for a dam and reservoir. When Father Crowley died in a car accident, authorities completed the Long Valley Dam and named the reservoir Lake Crowley. If it weren’t for his intervention, the lake wouldn’t have existed.

Sources indicate that as the years passed, visitors continued coming to Lake Crowley to fish, kayak, camp, and hike. Then something weird started to appear on the cliffsides. The banks appeared to be receding and hollowing out, revealing hundreds upon hundreds of spiral columns. Many onlookers believed they were man-made. Some compared the formations to Moorish architecture from North Africa and Spain.

In a recent development, though the reservoir is man-made, the area’s history dates back millennia. Crowley Lake lies in the wider Long Valley Caldera, one of Earth’s largest calderas.

Sources indicate that some of the columns. Photo: Shutterstock.

The caldera sits atop one of three ancient supervolcanoes in the United States. Around 760,000 years ago, this supervolcano erupted and spewed 650 cubic kilometers of rhyolite rock and ash into the air for a week. It covered the land in a blanket of ash and debris over one kilometer thick. And it left behind a 32km long, 18km wide, and 900m deep depression in the earth.

Recent findings suggest that the depression formed when the subterranean magma chamber emptied onto the surface and the remnant shell of a roof collapsed. The blast and pyroclastic flow were so powerful that ash fell as far as Kansas. Along the rim are the lava dome complexes of Mammoth, Glass, and Bald Mountains. The caldera also hosts a cluster of hydrothermally active lakes called the Mammoth Lakes.

Sources indicate that the main feature left by the eruption is the Bishop Tuff, a few square kilometers in area. A tuff is a rock of compacted volcanic ash. At the base of this tuff stand the Crowley Lake Columns. They range in thickness, average about six meters high, and are generally reddish, beige, grey, or white with a dark water line at their base. Some lean while others stand straight.

It has been revealed that attached by arches, the columns are so evenly spaced that to some visitors, it resembles an ancient temple. Horizontal cracks about 30cm apart add further detail to the columns. They look like they hold up the cliffs but they simply remained after the softer cliff rock started to erode.

Industry observers note that the high levels of silica, sodium, and potassium in the columns make the rock conduct heat well and cool suddenly. This led to the cracks. Similar formations exist in Guatemala, Mexico, and Newly introduced Mexico.

The few people who frequent Crowley Lake have long known about the columns. Only recently, social media has started to highlight them. This is due to its seclusion on the lake’s shoreline. The only ways to access them are on foot or by boat, kayak, or 4×4. The dirt road on which you turn from Highway 395 is so steep and uneven that it can bog down vehicle. Visitors tend to drive halfway, then walk.

It has been revealed that despite popular speculation that these columns are an example of columnar jointing, they are not. The geological process is different. With columnar jointing, the spaces are not so far apart. A study by geologists at UC Berkeley used a combination of computer models, X-ray diffraction, and electron microscope imagery to determine how they formed. It turns out that the culprit is simply…water.

“We hypothesize that the columns are a result of instabilities at the liquid water and steam interface as cold water seeped into the still-cooling Bishop Tuff,” indicates Noah Randolph-Flagg, the study’s lead scientist.

The columns formed through hydrothermal convection. Photo: Shutterstock.

Essentially, rainwater seeped down into the hot ash and started to boil, producing a mineral glue called mordonite. The boiling water formed a column of steam which carried the mordonite upward through the rock. Thus, the mineral hardened the rock, leading it to remain standing while the surrounding rock eroded. This process is called hydrothermal convection or circulation.

In a recent development, according to Randolph-Flagg, it only took 100 years to form these columns. The study also states that “the liquid water–steam interface probably is the source of the instability that generates columnar flow.”.

According to recent reports, as for the erosion of the cliffside, the reservoir’s water levels fluctuate throughout the year with the seasons. After the completion of the reservoir, the columns started to reveal themselves. The constant rise and fall as well as a repeating freeze-thaw cycle caused the tuff to recede. It revealed the columns and also hollowed out the cliffside to form shallow caves. Take care when going into these little caves or pushing on the columns, as they might not be as stable. As the cliff continues to erode, we should see more of these columns.

The arches resemble Moorish architecture. Photo: Shutterstock.

According to recent reports, in terms of the Long Valley Caldera, scientists have closely monitored its activity, which has been increasing since the 1980s. Since it is a one of only 20 supervolcanoes in the world, they have paid close attention to its potential for eruption, despite its status as inactive.

According to recent reports, there have been small earthquakes and signs of movement in the earth as if it were “breathing.” This is seen in Yellowstone, another supervolcano. While there are no immediate signs of an impending eruption, the caldera’s history and current activity suggest that it is possible.

#228545. Industry News: What Happens When You Come Home From Your Thru-Hike?

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1702 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: What Happens When You Come Home From Your Thru-Hike?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1702 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that this guest post was written by Amy “Yardsale” Johnson.
  • Recent findings suggest that there are endless articles, Youtube videos, books, and discussions about preparing for trail.
  • This question receives far less guidance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this guest post was written by Amy “Yardsale” Johnson. Full bio at the end.

Recent findings suggest that there are endless articles, Youtube videos, books, and discussions about preparing for trail. But what happens when we come back home?

This question receives far less guidance. But for many hikers, “coming home” is one of the hardest parts.

I thru-hiked the Appalachian Trail and hiked 1600 miles of the Continental Divide Trail, and I have felt the challenge of spending months on trail and then coming home to a “society” that feels so at odds with the trail experience.

How might we be able to carry the gifts of the trail with us and create a life and a world that is more deeply alive?

In a recent development, for months, we sleep beneath the stars, watch the Milky Way move across the sky, catch the sunrise, and feel the cool breeze of dawn, brimming over with possibility as birds greet the day. As we walk, carrying everything we need on our backs, demands and expectations fall away.

Sources indicate that there is no one left to impress, and no one left to be, other than our raw, unfiltered, beautiful selves. In this rawness and vulnerability, we meet each other. We walk, we talk, we sleep under the stars. We bear witness to one another’s stories, we hold one another up. We watch as the first flowers open in the spring, and then as the first leaves turn crimson, set on fire in the fall.

Recent findings suggest that somewhere along the way, we find deep connection with ourselves, with others, and with nature. We find more space, more color, more life. For the first time, perhaps, we have eyes to see.

We return to our jobs and routines, and the demands and expectations return too. Suddenly, how people interact with us is dependent on how we look, how much money we make, or where we’re from.

In a recent development, we’re expected to work, probably a lot of hours, cooped up indoors, often without a break. With little appreciation, perhaps little financial reward, and little connection to how our work might benefit people or nature. The core of who we are, which had emerged so quietly on trail, sometimes feels buried once again.

Sources indicate that I believe the connection and community that we experience on trail open up an incredible possibility. In returning home, we have a chance to carry these gifts with us. We have a chance to create a kinder and more beautiful world: a world with more space, more color, and more life. I believe we can start by rewriting our own lives, step by step, and then by participating in the rewriting of our own small corner of the world. And maybe, this journey is the most important trail of all.

We can begin by considering how we can incorporate small aspects of our experience into our everyday life (and then more, and more, until our lives are more and more aligned).

After all, it’s one step after another that allowed us to hike for hundreds, or thousands, of miles. Are our everyday lives really so different from the trail? Isn’t the natural world all around us? The birds, the flowers, the trees, right outside our windows? The people around us every day, are they not people just like people on trail?

And if people on trail can form supportive, inclusive, beautiful communities, why shouldn’t we also be able to do that in our daily lives?

We all have the power to act, to respond, to create something in this world. On trail, we persevere in the face of conditions that we have no control over: difficult weather, trail conditions, and the physical limitations of our body. Truly, we are small and weak in the face of the power and beauty of Mother Nature.

It has been revealed that but we have the power to respond, participate, and persevere. And as it turns out, that power ends up taking us pretty far. From Georgia to Maine, or Mexico to Canada, or any distance that we so choose.

Similarily, in society, we are all small and weak in the face of many of the powerful forces around us. Our culture, the economy, the govermment, and the people around us are all forces that we have little control over. But just like on trail, we always have the power to respond, to participate, and to persevere. And I believe that power can take us pretty far. To a better world, I venture to imagine.

I think we can get there by leaning into the same things that we leaned into on trail: community, perseverance, connection with nature, trust in ourselves, and other people.

Before hiking, I never thought I could hitchhike, that I could navigate remote wilderness on my own, or that I could literally walk from Georgia to Maine. I never imagined that I could break so many “rules” of our society. But I did, and what I found through that vulnerability was deep connection, deep love, faith, and an abiding confidence.

Might it be that we are playing by unspoken rules in our everyday lives that might be holding us back from true confidence, true connection, and latest possibilities?

What might happen if we start to question them, and connect anyway?

In a recent development, when we have an urgent need on trail, oftentimes we have no choice but to ask for help. So like it or not, we swallow our pride, get over our fears, and ask some stranger if they can help. Usually, they do, and gladly.

What might happen if we began to do that in our everyday lives? What might happen if we offered that same level of support to others?

What new possibilities might break open, once we begin to realize that the trail was never separate from society, nor was the end of our hike the end of our journey.

What if it was only the beginning?

What might the next steps look like in practice?

In a recent development, let’s start with a few questions to consider. Everyone has their own unique experience on trail, and chances are, no two hikers’ “return-home journeys” will be the same. Journaling is one tool that I’ve found helpful in processing my experiences.

According to recent reports, what did you experience on trail? How did you feel, and what upcoming perspectives did you find? What aspects of your hike contributed to feeling the way you did?

What perspectives or ways of being did you find on trail that you want to hold onto? What are some small steps you can take to incorporate those perspectives or ways of being into your daily life?

According to recent reports, additionally, below are some of the small practical changes that I’ve found helpful. Have your own practices? Add them to the conversation.

In a recent development, 1. Spend the first half hour or more of the day doing something just for you: outside and active is even better. This can set the tone for the entire day. The day belongs to you, to nature, to life itself. Everything else fits into that deeper truth.

3. Eat well (not like on trail, hah!).

It has been revealed that 4. Get outside regularly. It could be day hikes, weekend backpacking trips, or just taking in the sunlight for 5 minutes from your porch.

5. Along the lines of getting outside: connect with God, the universe, nature, or a sense of meaning beyond yourself.

6. Stay in touch with trail friends, and find like-minded people at home. Going on the post-trail journey with people “who get it” is immeasurably valuable.

In a recent development, 7. Find ways to have the authentic relationships like the ones you found on trail. How might you be able to give and receive help more freely, and be yourself without reserve, with the people closest to you?

8. Find joy in the small things. Maybe it’s a fresh bouquet of flowers from the farmers market, the sunlight streaming in through the window, or the birds chirping.

9. Think about how your work can contribute to others, to yourself, and to nature. Start to think about how you might be able to negotiate your work, or your relationship with work, to find better work-life balance, and/or a deeper sense of meaning and contribution. It doesn’t all have to be better all at once. Small steps in the right direction is all that’s needed.

10. Learn about money. Things like budgeting, the time value of money, how debt works, saving and investing. Like it or not, our world runs on money. Money is one of the major keys to more freedom in our world. Use it as a tool to create more space, joy, abundance, and freedom for yourself, your community, and nature.

Industry observers note that 11. Acceptance. Accepting things we can’t control allows us to have more peace. And we can lean into that which we can control: our response, which is powerful. Just like on trail.

In a recent development, amy “Yardsale” Johnson is a long-distance hiker, writer, speaker, retreat host, and founder of the Blue Compass Institute. She creates writing and experiences that break open possibilities so that people can create more deeply thriving and connected lives. Her work can be found at https://www.bluecompassinstitute.com, or follow along on Instagram @bluecompassinstitute.

Everest Winds Force Climbers to Retreat

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (511 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Despite weather forecasts of high winds on Everest, the Russian team gamely left for the West Shoulder today.
  • Industry observers note that “It’s calm right now, but the forecast is worrying,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote yesterday from a snow cave, where Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and Vasiliev had sheltered for the night at 6,400m.
  • The three climbers had fixed three pitches above them, according to Mountain Club, and were hoping for firmer terrain as they approached the West Shoulder of Everest, en route to the West Ridge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite weather forecasts of high winds on Everest, the Russian team gamely left for the West Shoulder today. But in the end, they couldn’t fight the gale-force winds, which eventually forced them back to their tent at the base of the mountain.

Industry observers note that “It’s calm right now, but the forecast is worrying,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote yesterday from a snow cave, where Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and Vasiliev had sheltered for the night at 6,400m. Late today, they confirmed that the weather forecast of powerful winds was unfortunately right.

The three climbers had fixed three pitches above them, according to Mountain Club, and were hoping for firmer terrain as they approached the West Shoulder of Everest, en route to the West Ridge.

However, as we previously reported after consulting meteorologist Vitor Baia of Portugal, conditions were good Tuesday and Wednesday, but winds rose dramatically today.

On a previous foray up Everest, one of the climbers heads for the West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

It has been revealed that “The winds are very strong,” Vasiliev reported. “It is impossible to work higher on the mountain.”.

Vasiliev said that his team is retreating to a tent at 5,600m. This is below the Lho La Pass, possibly on the Khumbu Glacier beside the vertical section leading to that col.

The question is whether the team will wait there for better conditions, retreat to their base in Lobuche, or call off the expedition.

Some charts still show a chance of variable winds tomorrow, before the jet stream hits the mountain with full force (see below).

Wind levels at around summit altitude on Everest this week, by meteoexploration.com.

Baia says the winds will remain high every day until next Tuesday. From Wednesday on, the winds should be weaker.

The Russians set off on their third trip up Everest last Monday, hoping to summit via the West Ridge without oxygen or external support, and with no one else on the mountain.

In a recent development, on Tuesday evening, they checked in with Mountain Club from their tent at 6,000m, where they spent the night. The hard trailbreaking through fresh snow had slowed their pace, but they expected better conditions on the following day, as they started up steeper terrain toward Everest’s shoulder. They knew the snow up there was harder and compacted. They could even see their trails from the previous trip up, so no new soft snow had accumulated.

The Russian team on Everest’s West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

It has been revealed that yesterday, Vasiliev noted that they had climbed four pitches on old fixed ropes, plus another eight pitches of their own. The team is fixing ropes at the hardest sections, but not entirely along the route. As expected, snow conditions had improved with the more vertical terrain, but as Vasiliev pointed out, “it’s not exactly easy walking yet.”.

Industry observers note that the Russian leader insists the route to the summit is doable. However, wind delays and a lack of time may ultimately end their attempt.

#228541. Piolet d'Or Team Shares Insider Tips for Climbing in Peru's Huayhuash Range

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1282 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Piolet d'Or Team Shares Insider Tips for Climbing in Peru's Huayhuash Range

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1282 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Marc Toralles, Ruben Sanmartin, and Bru Busom of Spain were awarded a Piolet d’Or for a highly committing fresh route on Yerupaja Grande (6,634m), the highest peak of Peru’s Huayhuash range.
  • According to recent reports, in the last few years, the Andes have reportedly been affected by climate change.
  • “That means that climbers need to pick their route carefully [when judging] what lingers above them,” Buson explained.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Marc Toralles, Ruben Sanmartin, and Bru Busom of Spain were awarded a Piolet d’Or for a highly committing fresh route on Yerupaja Grande (6,634m), the highest peak of Peru’s Huayhuash range. ExplorersWeb asked the young climbers about the ascent and the unique character of the Andes. They offered some tips for climbers looking to add Peru to their list of high-altitude destinations.

According to recent reports, in the last few years, the Andes have reportedly been affected by climate change. “The main effect is that the huge snow structures on the summits are exposed to warmer temperatures and become more fragile,” Sanmartin stated. “Basically, they fall down more easily.”.

“That means that climbers need to pick their route carefully [when judging] what lingers above them,” Buson explained.

Bru Buson, left, and Marc Toralles. Photo: Ruben Sanmartin.

This was especially noticeable last year on Siula Grande. “There was a snowfield midway up the face as we trekked by, and on our way back, it was not there anymore,” said Marc Toralles. “Somehow, the melting process in the Andes, with its 5,000m and even 6,000m [altitudes], is similar to what we are seeing every year in the Alps, where we all work as mountain guides.”.

Industry observers note that for Toralles, the best thing in the Andes is how accessible the mountains are. “It’s so easy to go climbing there,” he mentioned.

It has been revealed that there are no lifts or paved roads, but you can go, climb a peak, and return in three or four days. Something like that in the Himalaya would take weeks. All you need is to get to Huaraz by plane, bus, or car from Lima, where you may stay some days to acclimatize (there are many options), and then go to the mountains.

If your planned peak is not in the right conditions, you will surely find some other one to climb. Also, the options are infinite for ice climbing, alpine climbing, rock, trekking, anything.

The team’s base camp. Photo: Spanish Yerupaja Grande team.

Industry observers note that red tape is minimal. There are no permits for peaks. Instead, climbers and trekkers pay a small fee to cross the comunidades (the areas) where they want to climb, and climbers can hire arrieros (riders with mules) to help carry equipment and supplies to base camps or higher. On this occasion, the climbers kept their logistics basic, with little beyond a slightly larger base camp tent.

With some of the more accessible places, it is advisable to have someone watching over your base camp while you are away climbing.

Sources indicate that once you leave the beaten track, you’ll be alone. “There are no crowds in Huayhuash,” Buson stated. Why aren’t they more popular? The climbers explained that Huayhuash peaks are typically more difficult than popular options in the Cordillera Blanca, also in Peru. But they note this lack of popularity is changing fast. “We are seeing much more people in recent years, both climbing and trekking,” they said.

Sources indicate that thanks to the many possibilities, the three Spanish climbers didn’t need to do much planning. “We know Huayhuash pretty well, we are familiar with the terrain and the climbing style, and we are aware there are always options,” said Toralles, who has climbed there four times.

That said, the line the Spaniards climbed on Yerupaja last year was not improvised. They had that route in their mind for some time. “We heard of someone who had tried but called the attempt off, so the route was there to be climbed,” Toralles said. “In addition, it didn’t require a long time, and the timing worked for me, since I was traveling to Peru anyway to do some guiding.”.

Recent findings suggest that buson and Sanmartin joined immediately. To acclimatize, they had worked double shifts the previous weeks around Chamonix, where both are professional guides. “Working on the Mont Blanc massif intensively was great training and acclimatization,” they said. “We were ready by the time we set foot on the mountain.”.

The best time to climb in Huayhuash is July, August, and the first half of September.

Once on the mountain, they carefully checked the conditions of the face and the line they would follow. “In the Andes, you have to assume that the summit ridge snow formations, the famous ‘mushrooms,’ the substantial cornices, and the seracs on the sides of the face are mostly in a delicate state. You need to assume that you will progress on deep, unstable snow, and the entire structure may have deteriorated and be prone to crumble,” Buson noted.

In a recent development, to deal with them, the climbers used some custom-made tools: They attached alitas (little wings) to their ice axes for a better grip on foamy, loose snow. They also carried small snowshoes for some sections.

Ice axe with ‘alitas’ (wings). Photo: Nick Sheldon/Mountain Project.

Conditions in the Andean mountains are always variable. “You’ll find different terrain depending on the altitude and the orientation,” Sanmartin added. “This is why technical routes on these peaks require a high level of commitment, which, as happened on our route, may be even higher than the intrinsic difficulty of the pitches,” Toralles explained.

With this in mind, the Spanish team named the route they opened Essence of Commitment.

In a recent development, marc Toralles ready for the ridge, with large snow pickets and an ice axe with ‘wings’ attached. Photo: Buson/Sanmartin.

Recent findings suggest that in this sort of terrain, it is paramount to stay focused and make the right call between subjective and objective factors. “There are countless reasons to turn around on climbs like this, but one must keep going, except for obvious reasons, such as an injury, a completely impassable section, or a really violent storm,” Sanmartin mentioned.

“That is why it is important to consider all options and potential issues before starting the climb. You need to be sure you like the line and want to climb it.”.

Asked whether they reached a point of no return during their climb, Buson admitted they did. “On reaching the ridge, we became aware that trying to downclimb the same route would be quite complex. However, we also saw the route upward was doable.”.

According to recent reports, the Spaniards did not count on a professional meteorologist. “We had our friends texting us the online, free forecasts over InReach,” they stated. “One of the positive aspects of Huayhuash is that good weather periods tend to last for quite a while. Weather windows of five to six days are common.” During their climb, for example, they enjoyed acceptable weather, with some rain and snow but no high winds.

Industry observers note that they warn that conditions in the Andes are changing promptly. “You need to observe the mountains and adapt,” Toralles said. “Some people aim for a route based on the information in a guidebook printed 50 years ago, and find a totally different scenario.” He pointed out that Siula Grande looked different in 2025 than it did when he climbed it just three years earlier.

Sanmartin noted that conditions have also changed on normal routes. They are now drier, more complex, and often more hazardous. “In some cases, climbers are abandoning the normal routes up the glaciers and opt for ridges which may be more difficult but in better conditions,” he said.

The climbers think the Andes will not get as crowded as the Himalaya, simply because the logistics are not as advanced — no refuges, no helicopters — and because they don’t have the sizzle of being the tallest peaks on Earth. “But they have incredible potential,” they stated.

#228538. A Man Just Ran 3,015 Miles From San Francisco to Newly introduced York in 41 Days, Setting New Record

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (650 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

A Man Just Ran 3,015 Miles From San Francisco to Newly introduced York in 41 Days, Setting New Record

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (650 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When Cameron Balser left San Francisco at 4:59 a.m.
  • Sources indicate that his crossing beat the previous transcontinental record by more than seven hours and cleared the 42-day mark with just over seven hours to spare.
  • Recent findings suggest that the final push in New York.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Cameron Balser left San Francisco at 4:59 a.m. on October 10, he set out to run the 3,015-mile Trans America route across the United States in under 42 days in pursuit of a fresh transcontinental record. About six weeks later, he reached New York City Hall in lower Manhattan at 11:45 p.m. on Friday, November 20, finishing in 41 days, 16 hours, 46 minutes, and 45 seconds.

Sources indicate that his crossing beat the previous transcontinental record by more than seven hours and cleared the 42-day mark with just over seven hours to spare. For the final stretch down Manhattan’s West Side Drive, a large group of supporters ran alongside him to the finish.

Recent findings suggest that the final push in New York. Photo via Bernie Bernstein.

Data collected during the run reveals how Balser broke the record due to consistency. Over the 42 days, he averaged 72.1 miles per day with a median pace of 74.5 miles per day. He hit at least 70 miles on 33 of his 42 days and crossed the 75-mile threshold 18 times.

Sources indicate that on his third day, Balser logged his biggest climb of the entire crossing, gaining 14,210 feet of elevation over 69 miles. By the time he reached Manhattan, he had accumulated 148,546 feet of total vertical gain. Balser ran 500 miles in 6.4 days, 1,000 miles in 13 days, and 2,000 miles in 27.2 days.

Balser’s only notable slowdown came in early November, when he recorded his shortest day of the crossing at 42.2 miles in 10 hours and 10 minutes, followed by 45.5 miles the next day and 59.4 miles on November 9. However, by November 12, he had returned to a 75-mile day. In the following week, which would mark the end of his attempt, Balser covered 542.5 miles, averaging 77.5 miles per day. By comparison, his opening week totaled 504.7 miles at a 72.1-mile daily average.

Recent findings suggest that cameron Balser in Fresh York City. Photo via Bernie Bernstein.

According to recent reports, his final day into Upcoming York City was the biggest push of the entire run. On that day, Balser covered 91.8 miles in 18 hours and 48 minutes, which also was his only day surpassing 80 miles.

At the end of the run, Balser focused on the motivation behind the miles rather than the clock.

Industry observers note that “It was very humbling in a lot of ways. I wanted people to know how beautiful they already are and how loved they are,” Balser stated. “Getting that message out by running 75+ miles a day is more notable than the record. That’s why I did this, to show people how beautiful they are.”.

It has been revealed that looking at the crowd that turned out for his late-night arrival in New York, he added: “I did not expect that many people to come out, it was a surreal moment… I went back to the memories of the people who helped us. I just really appreciated everyone’s help.”.

Lucky Skier Survives Night in Crevasse With Two Broken Legs

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (283 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thirty-nine-year-old Emeric Ossatte was ski touring alone earlier this week in the Savoie area of the French Alps, near the Italian border.
  • Sources indicate that the Grenoble-area man, who wasn’t carrying a beacon or radio, doffed his backpack and crawled 100m through the crevasse, looking for a way out.
  • According to a Facebook report by France’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue unit, they saw the slide path but no immediate sign of Ossatte.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thirty-nine-year-old Emeric Ossatte was ski touring alone earlier this week in the Savoie area of the French Alps, near the Italian border. He removed his skis to posthole up a steep couloir in his boots and crampons when an avalanche swept him downhill, depositing him into a crevasse and breaking both his legs.

Sources indicate that the Grenoble-area man, who wasn’t carrying a beacon or radio, doffed his backpack and crawled 100m through the crevasse, looking for a way out. But the sides of the crack were too steep, and there was no cell service where he was. He remained beside an air pocket in the crevasse overnight. Meanwhile, when he didn’t check in that evening, his family raised the alarm.

According to a Facebook report by France’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue unit, they saw the slide path but no immediate sign of Ossatte. The search continued until the middle of the night, when avalanche risk forced the rescuers to suspend their operations.

The following morning, a large contingent of 28 ground rescuers, dogs, three helicopters, and a physician to tend to Ossatte, if they found him alive, converged on the site, according to France 3. They found his gear and dug for five hours until they heard him calling out.

According to recent reports, “He was really lucky,” stated Major Yoann Haberey of the mountain-rescue team. “We knew he was under there. But we didn’t think we’d find him alive.”.

According to recent reports, by the time they extracted him, he had been there almost a day and a half. The hypothermic but lucky survivor was flown to the hospital for treatment and surgery on one of his legs.

Weekend Warm-Up: Behind the Climb

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (428 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As the title suggests, Behind the Climb brings viewers behind the scenes with Colin Haley and Tyler Karow as they take on the Southeast Ridge of Cerro Torre.
  • Sources indicate that as the short film opens, Haley introduces us to the route in voiceover, while on-screen, he and Karow make the approach, crossing ice fields and fording streams.
  • The Headwall section of Cerro Torre.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As the title suggests, Behind the Climb brings viewers behind the scenes with Colin Haley and Tyler Karow as they take on the Southeast Ridge of Cerro Torre. Colin Haley has tried the route, which he calls a modern classic, three times already without success. He hopes that by teaming up with Tyler Karow, the fourth time will be the charm.

Sources indicate that as the short film opens, Haley introduces us to the route in voiceover, while on-screen, he and Karow make the approach, crossing ice fields and fording streams. The route is divided into three main sections: the Haston Crack, Ice Towers, and Headwall. Haley was turned back twice by bad weather on the Ice Towers; neither of them has finished the Headwall.

The Headwall section of Cerro Torre. Photo: Screenshot.

In a recent development, hoping to catch the Ice Towers still frozen and the Headwall still warmed by the sun, they wake up so early that the sun hasn’t actually finished setting yet. At that point, it seems more accurate to say that they took an evening nap and then climbed through the night.

Sources indicate that interspersed with clips of climbing, Haley and Karow review the footage, sharing the little logistical details and impressions of the climb. The Ice Towers, which Karow recalls attempting many years ago, have changed since he last encountered them. Once, as the name implies, thick with ice, much of it has now melted. “In another ten years,” Karow predicts, they will “look drastically different.”.

Ice or no, they complete the second section. This time, the weather cooperates. Haley takes over for the final section, the dastardly Headwall which has repeatedly eluded him. The climbing itself is going well, but melting snow above is making the rock run with water. This, he admits, is a significant disadvantage to their carefully timed strategy.

Despite the wet holds, Haley makes good progress. With only a few pitches to go, the self-described pessimist Haley admits that he finally thinks they’ll make it to the top. When he does finally reach the summit, grinning widely at the camera, voiceover reveals he has already started worrying about the descent.

In a recent development, keeping with the promise to go behind the scenes, the video doesn’t stop at the summit, where they stand victoriously and admire the views. We follow the pair as they rappel down.

At the bottom, when asked how they feel about the adventure, both men reply simply that their hands hurt. Not all of us can be poets.

#228529. Trail Marshall vs. Troll Marshal, Gifts for Hikers, and Who’s a Hiker Bro | This Week on Trail #3

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1105 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Trail Marshall vs. Troll Marshal, Gifts for Hikers, and Who’s a Hiker Bro | This Week on Trail #3

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1105 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Trail Marshall has 88,000 Facebook followers, a bio promising love and positivity, and calls the Appalachian Trail a “Bourbon Street in the woods.”.
  • According to recent reports, on this episode of This Week on Trail, produced by The Trek, hosts Jess “Sassafras” and Katie “Double Dip” try to decide whether he’s a whistleblower or a professional rage-baiter, and what to make of the Facebook parody group built to mock him.
  • Trail Marshall is one of the most-followed thru-hiking personalities on Facebook, with a bio listing the Mountains-to-Sea Trail, the Benton MacKaye, and AT hikes in 2020, 2021, 2023, and 2025.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Trail Marshall has 88,000 Facebook followers, a bio promising love and positivity, and calls the Appalachian Trail a “Bourbon Street in the woods.”.

According to recent reports, on this episode of This Week on Trail, produced by The Trek, hosts Jess “Sassafras” and Katie “Double Dip” try to decide whether he’s a whistleblower or a professional rage-baiter, and what to make of the Facebook parody group built to mock him. Plus, gift picks from The Trek’s holiday guides, a survey comment section demanding justice for SOBOs, a Hiker Bro Quiz showdown, and a listener tip about a beloved Newly introduced York shelter that the hosts couldn’t confirm.

Trail Marshall is one of the most-followed thru-hiking personalities on Facebook, with a bio listing the Mountains-to-Sea Trail, the Benton MacKaye, and AT hikes in 2020, 2021, 2023, and 2025. Jess, who brought the story, describes him as someone some hikers call infamous and others call a whistleblower, and notes he seems to enjoy being controversial. Katie says she’s not in the whistleblower camp, but she can’t open Facebook without reading his latest rant all the way through.

Jess walks through his “Toxic Truths of the Appalachian Trail” series, which he says will become a book (both hosts proposal to buy it). In installments like “AT Scam Culture,” Trail Marshall alleges that most hostels and shuttles are grifters or opportunists, criticizes some for-profit trail angels, and regularly calls out the ATC and ALDHA. He also describes the trail south of Fresh Jersey as a “Bourbon Street in the woods” and alleges an organized drug network that protects dangerous people, even recasting the community’s practice of circulating photos of men who make women uncomfortable as a way of punishing drug mules. Katie grants that the AT likely sees more crime than other trails because it runs so close to population centers, and the hosts are openly skeptical of the drug-mule theory.

Then there are the haters. Jess explains that critics built a Facebook group called the Troll Marshal Community, posting AI parody comics of his likeness and thinly veiled jabs dressed up as trail etiquette tips. The group has since been taken down, and Trail Marshall states it was removed because it was illegal harassment, calling it cyberbullying and cyberstalking and alleging that hiking organizations shared it. Jess says she saw no evidence of that last claim, and that mocking a real person this way is a messed-up thing to do. Along the way, there’s a story about someone Venmo-ing him pennies just to send mean messages, and a debate over what it would cost to insult each host.

In a recent development, neither host can tell how much Trail Marshall believes and how much is engagement strategy. Katie notices that his most enthusiastic commenters rarely seem to be thru-hikers saying his claims match their own experience, and Jess points to a recent run of posts about missing hikers and possible serial killers on the AT, some involving crimes with no clear tie to the trail, that she calls borderline fearmongering. Both agree there’s a real conversation to have about crime and situational awareness on trail, just not one that tells people the AT is too dangerous to hike. Jess also relives the night her own face demonstrated up on his page, and the hosts want to hear what listeners think.

Sources indicate that trek writers and Bloggers weighed in on this year’s gift guides, and each host picks two favorites. Jess starts with Superfeet insoles ($50), a stocking stuffer for hikers with foot pain that she suggests gifting with a receipt, since the right model depends on the foot, and follows with the Kindle Paperwhite, the splurge she packs for reading at camp because her eyes tire on a phone screen. Katie picks Fillo’s Walking Tamales ($35 for seven), a shelf-stable snack both hosts have been eating, though Katie wishes it packed more protein (a flavor taste test is apparently in the works). Her other pick is the $12 Chicken Tramper Ultralight Gear Bear Can Key, which she started using early in her CDT hike and calls a rare true game changer for the price.

A Trek video recapping stats from the 2025 AT Thru-Hiker Survey drew comments less about the data than about the deadline. Jess, who works with the survey data, agrees that closing it in early November shortchanges SOBOs and flip-floppers still on trail, and announces an extended deadline. She also agrees that 279 responses is a small sample and wants many more hikers to take part, while both hosts push back on a commenter who says section hikers are ignored: the survey is designed to help future thru-hikers blueprint, though long-section hikers can still contribute.

In a latest segment, the hosts take on a Spotify comment about the crying-baby-at-a-campground episode that called out “two childless women” for joking about suffocating babies. They concede the “childless women” part is factually accurate, acknowledge that the jokes won’t land for everyone, and apologize, then offer the commenter one free shot at their own insecurities, which detours into a cat-flea saga.

A Backpacker Radio clip has Zach taking the Hiker Bro Quiz from Eliza “Swerve” Sweeney, landing at 45% bro after admitting he eats coffee powder with no water. Katie scored 60%, officially a “certified hiker bro,” though she’d rather call herself “a bro in good standing.”.

According to recent reports, listener Jimbo writes in that Ralph’s Peak Hikers’ Cabin, the RPH Shelter in New York and one of the few spots on the AT where you can get a pizza delivered, is slated for demolition in mid-2027. The hosts couldn’t find anything online to confirm it, so if you know more, send it their way.

Katie joins Zach and Andrew Skurka for Backpacker Radio LIVE in Denver on December 5 (ugly holiday sweaters encouraged), and Jess invites anyone planning a long-distance hike in 2027 to apply to blog for The Trek.

#228524. Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1695 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1695 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak.
  • It has been revealed that gribbin released his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2.
  • The journey has not gone according to proposal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak. But relentless weather delays and mounting costs have made the journey even more challenging than anticipated.

It has been revealed that gribbin released his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2. Paddling clockwise, he has covered 2,584km. From Crinan, he continued up the west coast of Scotland and around Cape Wrath and Duncansby Head before heading south along the eastern and southern coasts. His latest reported landing point is Cliff End, near Hastings, Sussex.

The journey has not gone according to proposal. Persistent Atlantic weather systems have cost him weeks of paddling time, while the financial demands of keeping the expedition moving have forced him to return to freelance television camerawork so he and his wife, Nicola, can keep it running.

While he paddles, she follows him in their motor home, offering shore support. He now hopes to complete the circle at Crinan in the spring of 2027. ExplorersWeb caught up with him to find out more about the journey. This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

How do you approach the daily distances on a journey like this?

Given that circumnavigating the British mainland is at least 3,700km, I have aimed to do at least 40km per day. My longest day so far has been 64km. However, weather, tides and daylight length, particularly in autumn and winter, often curtail one’s best-laid plans. Some days have been necessarily shorter, forcing me to make an earlier-than-envisaged retreat to shore.

Industry observers note that but this is very much a journey, not a race, so we will continue into the spring of 2027. It’s an incredible opportunity to explore every nook and cranny of the GB coastline.

How much has the weather affected your progress?

Roughly 85% of delays have been due to poor weather, 5% to Ministry of Defense firing range timetable restrictions, and 10% to the need for very specific tidal windows to navigate particular sections safely and efficiently. I have never had a delay due to fatigue or the need for a break from the sheer physical nature of this endurance challenge. I have used days when I have inevitably been “weathered-off” to recoup my energy reserves.

Recent findings suggest that for most of the trip, it has been extremely rare to have more than four days of consistently good paddling weather. Setting off from Crinan on June 2 meant we did not enjoy the heat wave experienced in southern Britain. Instead, we lost at least six weeks to poor weather. Constant Atlantic westerly and northwesterly fronts brought wind, rain, and high seas that seemed to permanently batter northwest and northern Scotland throughout June, July, and even into early August. It was one of the great untalked-about weather phenomena of summer 2026. It wasn’t all heat waves…at least not in Scotland!

Are you camping or sleeping in the motorhome?

Industry observers note that northwest Scotland and its wild, deeply indented coastline often made road access to the sea impossible. Early on, we accepted that there would be long stretches when Nicola would not see me for over 24 hours. She was often doing double the mileage I was doing and negotiating some very hairy driving conditions on roads way off the beaten track. That resulted in many planned and unplanned wild camps along the coast.

By the time we reached the north coast of Scotland, road access had improved dramatically, and Nicola and I were generally able to coordinate to meet at the end of each day. This has proved an invaluable motivator, especially when the going gets tough. Our little motorhome has been a blessed retreat each night since then: a warm, reassuring space to relax, gather one’s thoughts, and blueprint ahead.

Recent findings suggest that the route so far. The blue line indicates the paddling route, the red line shows the route taken by the support vehicle. Image: Dominic Gribbin.

What kayak are you paddling, and how much equipment do you carry?

Industry observers note that I am paddling around Britain in a Rockpool Taran 16 sea kayak. It is a fast, beautifully handmade sea kayak, perfect for putting down the miles and handling heavy seas. The trade-off is stability, but it has a prodigious load capacity in its various watertight bulkheads.

I carry a kayak trolley permanently on the back deck. I have already worn out two and am constantly experimenting with fresh designs to better negotiate the challenges of gravel and sand beaches. As a minimum, I carry basic wild-camping equipment in case I need to spend an unexpected night ashore.

Food consists of pre-cooked rice bags, canned fish and vegetables, alongside plenty of snacks. I favor savory rather than sweet food. Coffee is my essential luxury, and I normally carry a can or two of beer!

Safety equipment is extensive. I carry a Garmin 86i Marine GPS with InReach satellite tracking, an ICOM marine handheld VHF radio with AIS and GPS, a spare VHF radio, flares and smoke signals, and a McMurdo personal locator beacon. I also carry a fully integrated Garmin Fenix 7 Pro watch, first-aid kit, spare paddles, compass, mobile phone, battery packs, head lamp, repair tape, and a Swiss Army penknife.

It has been revealed that the kayak itself weighs 24.9kg, but the overall weight, including my dry suit, buoyancy aid, clothing, and equipment, easily reaches 35kg or more. It is a significant challenge to negotiate all this weight over an often-unfriendly shoreline. However, the kayak benefits from the additional weight when afloat.

What have been the most memorable moments along the way?

We have had numerous encounters with sea otters, hunting pods of bottlenose dolphins, and close-up encounters with bottlenose mothers and calves. There have also been golden eagles and white-tailed sea eagles, the largest raptor in the UK. Some of the most sublime moments have been the inshore sea passages through the sheltered waters of the Inner Hebrides.

Successfully rounding Cape Wrath was a truly intimidating but awe-inspiring milestone. Then there was rounding the infamous Duncansby Head and crossing the Pentland Firth near John O’Groats, finally seeing the compass turn south. The huge breeding seabird colonies off Caithness and much of Scotland’s northeast coast have been incredible. Literally tens of thousands of birds, a deafening cacophony of noise!

Right along the GB coastline, we have also met some of the warmest and most generous people.

Have there been any particularly frightening moments?

Industry observers note that the huge seas off Strathy Point, Caithness, are probably the closest call yet. If something had gone wrong there while two kilometers offshore in those seas, I wouldn’t be writing this.

I have experienced plenty of rough and scary seas so far, but that occasion was another order of magnitude. They were enormous seas driven by Arctic swell and spring tides. They were the biggest seas I have ever paddled in. I am not in a rush to return there, despite its beauty.

In a recent development, you have mentioned that you are now combining freelance work with the expedition. How are you managing the financial and logistical side?

In a recent development, we were able to make this happen because I am self-employed. We bankrolled the expedition using our savings. The motorhome for shore support was the biggest investment. We initially calculated finances based on finishing by mid-autumn, but those weather delays cost us dearly. We ran out of money by mid-September, so I have had to return to my freelance work as a TV cameraman and juggle that with keeping this Edge of Britain expedition going until we are finished.

It has been revealed that there is no stopping this winter. Instead, we will take advantage of every weather window.

How did you first get into the sport?

I began paddling at age 11 when I permanently borrowed a friend’s old kayak and started exploring the ankle-deep waters of the River Ver and River Colne around St. Albans and Park Street, Hertfordshire. At 13, I started British Canoe Union training. This began my lifelong involvement with whitewater paddling on rivers around the world.

Sources indicate that back in the 1970s and 1980s, when I began, skills progression was funneled entirely through very actively encouraged participation in canoe slalom. Everybody who learned to paddle at club level was involved in slalom to some degree. I chose men’s C1 (Canadian singles) and competed at a national level, ranking 19th in Great Britain by the age of 18.

Industry observers note that university changed my orientation somewhat, and the allure of traveling to exotic whitewater rivers around the world took over. Expedition whitewater paddling then became my life, and still is, alongside expedition sea kayaking. Combining this with filmmaking ultimately led directly to my career as a television cameraman.

Why did you decide to take on a circumnavigation of Britain?

According to recent reports, the decision to attempt to paddle around the GB mainland is the culmination of a life spent kayaking. It is hard not to fall in love with the sheer beauty and allure of the world of the river and coastline, particularly here at home in the UK. This country has what is widely celebrated as some of the best sea kayaking in the world. To dream of exploring the whole GB coastline in as much detail as time and weather allow is, to me, a logical conclusion.

The actual decision came extremely late in the day, namely January 2026. This began a frantic period of organization ahead of our June 2 launch. Admittedly, April would have been better, but prior commitments meant we had to begin in June.

Industry observers note that I chose a clockwise route around Britain, thinking (naively) that the prevailing winds would vaguely be behind us for at least half the journey. I also wanted to tackle the potentially most technically demanding section of the northwest and north coast of Scotland early, in the height of what I envisaged as long summer days. How wrong I was!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • My name is Emilie and I am originally from flat land Ontario in Canada, but now I work as a nurse in beautiful British Columbia.
  • “Flat land” Ontario at 1000ft – top of Sleeping Giant.
  • Though I love day hiking, I have never done a long distance thru-hike.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that hey hikers!! My name is Emilie and I am originally from flat land Ontario in Canada, but now I work as a nurse in beautiful British Columbia. I am hiking the Pacific Crest Trail in 2027 which is why I am here, because my friends and family will all be wondering where I am, so it is easier to give updates this way.

“Flat land” Ontario at 1000ft – top of Sleeping Giant.

Though I love day hiking, I have never done a long distance thru-hike. I grew up car camping in Ontario and I have recently fallen in love with backpacking through mountains. I have hiked the West Coast Trail in BC and I am going to hike the W-trek in Patagonia in early 2027. I have always loved the outdoors and being active, which is why I have chosen to thru-hike in 2027.

Other than my outdoor hobbies, I am getting more into crafts such as crocheting and painting. One of my goals one day is to get a small watercolour book and paint the scenery of places I have hiked to! I don’t think that is very ultralight though, so perhaps I will save that for my post-PCT trail life.

I am a travel nurse, which means that I constantly move from town to town to work in under-serviced hospitals, so I am never in the same place for longer than a month. I regularly live out of a suitcase, so down-sizing to a backpack shouldn’t be too hard for me! I already know what my essentials are and have learned to not pack my fears into my suitcases.

According to recent reports, I choose to work in rural British Columbia, which means I am lucky to see the rugged and less tourist-heavy regions of BC. I am writing this post from North Vancouver Island, which has one of the highest cougar concentrations in the world, though I have yet to see one. I am hoping that won’t be one of the “firsts” I get to experience on the PCT.

Views from rural British Columbia – not a bad place to work.

Recent findings suggest that other than the obvious which is that hiking is better than working, the short version is that I am hiking because I can. Unfortunately, I do see a lot of sick patients in my job, a lot are older however some are young. I have learned from my patients that life is worth living when you are healthy and capable of experiencing it. “Do it while your body allows you” as they always say.

Society tells you that you need to work hard while you are young to enjoy your retirement. I see so many recent retirees dying, and wonder if they truly got to do the things that make them happy in life. On hard trail days, I will think of patients who aren’t able to be out there. Stay tuned for a future post going more in depth regarding my reasons to hike.

No-Oxygen Team Will Try Again on Everest

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (382 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Last week, high winds forced the Russian team to retreat from their third trip up the West Ridge of Everest.
  • “We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast.
  • Recent findings suggest that in a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last week, high winds forced the Russian team to retreat from their third trip up the West Ridge of Everest. Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and leader Andrei Vasiliev were climbing without oxygen, with no one else on the mountain. Winter is quickly approaching, but they have no intention of going home yet.

“We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast. Still want to try again,” Vasiliev texted to ExplorersWeb over the weekend. The climbers had not intended to reach the summit on that latest attempt up the West Shoulder of Everest via the Lho La Pass. Vasiliev explained that they were not yet acclimatized enough to reach the top without bottled oxygen. They did expect to reach higher than before, but high winds made that impossible.

Recent findings suggest that in a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up. On November 11, the team set off from their tent at the base of the West Ridge, fixing ropes in bitterly cold temperature. Contrary to forecasts, winds were light. The climbers pitched their tent at 6,500m and still had time to fix some ropes above them.

On the following morning, however, the gusts were too strong. After waiting in vain for the gale to abate, and with a forecast of even stronger winds the following day, Kondrashkin returned to the ridge, trying not to be blown away. He advanced between gusts and retrieved his two ice axes and the rope he had left behind the day before. They would need that gear for the descent.

Recent findings suggest that once at the bivouac, the climbers retrieved their tent, cached some food and fuel, and downclimbed to their Camp 1 at some 5,600m. It lies on the steep section between the Khumbu Glacier and the Lho La. Here, they pitched their tent again.

On Friday, the Russian team rappelled down to the glacier, on a “relatively safe” line to the right, where an avalanche fell as they descended.

Recent findings suggest that today, the team sits at their lodge in Lobuche and looks intently at weather forecasts. “We have not yet decided when to return to the mountain,” Vasiliev told Explorersweb. “It’s all about the weather, and the forecasts announce high winds on November 20-21.”.

Officials Blame Climate Change for Glacier Collapse That Killed 17

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (331 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Russian authorities are now attributing the September 6 disaster on 5,047m Mount Mizhirgi in the northern Caucasus to climate-related destabilization of a hanging glacier.
  • A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10.
  • The impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Russian authorities are now attributing the September 6 disaster on 5,047m Mount Mizhirgi in the northern Caucasus to climate-related destabilization of a hanging glacier.

A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10. Another 10 were unharmed and made it down the mountain on their own.

The impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them. As we reported at the time, helicopter pilot Alexander Davydov caught the avalanche on video.

Eldar Khashkhozhev of the Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations explained that warmer temperatures melted the protective blanket of snow, exposing parts of the glacier. This weakened the ice support that had glued enormous masses of snow and ice in place for decades.

A helicopter inspection of the region’s snow conditions the month before found no cause for concern, and some officials insist the catastrophe was unpredictable. However, climber Dmitry Polyakov, who was in the region at the time, disputed the idea that the glacier posed no danger. He remarked climbers had long recognized its instability and generally avoided approaching it in large groups.

Sources indicate that the Mizhirgi Glacier against Mizhirgi East and West peaks, site of September’s catastrophic glacial collapse. Photo: Shutterstock.

The key points of Khashkhozhev’s explanation were:.

Rising temperatures have raised the altitude of permanent snow cover.

Previously protected sections of the glacier became exposed, weakening the supporting ice beneath the hanging masses.

Eventually, gravity overcame that support and triggered a collapse that struck the training group.

This was the largest climbing disaster in the country since 2002, when another glacier collapse in North Ossetia, located between the Black and Caspian Seas, killed 125 people, including local residents.

With major landslides in summer and the possibility of glacial collapse at other times of the year throughout the world, mountaineers will have to adjust their behavior, as previously safe areas become potentially deadly.

Never-Say-Die Climbers Will Try Everest Again This Weekend

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Despite a forecast of high winds on November 21 and 22, Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have decided to begin a new attempt on the West Ridge of Everest on Sunday.
  • The three stubborn Russians will again proceed via the West Ridge without bottled oxygen, support, or any other living soul on the mountain.
  • The forecasts warn of very high winds all weekend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite a forecast of high winds on November 21 and 22, Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have decided to begin a new attempt on the West Ridge of Everest on Sunday.

The three stubborn Russians will again proceed via the West Ridge without bottled oxygen, support, or any other living soul on the mountain.

The forecasts warn of very high winds all weekend. Nevertheless, they will start up on Sunday, November 22, although that is the day with the strongest winds forecast.

Sources indicate that “That day, we will remain low on the mountain and climb to our Camp 1 at 5,600m,” Sergey Kondrashkin wrote. “From there, we will push upward when the weather improves and the winds die down, aiming to descend around November 28.”.

In a recent development, this means the team does not intend to summit quite yet. The goal is to acclimatize by reaching 7,500m and then return to their headquarters in Lobuche.

“The question is, will we manage to complete the summit push within the time frame of our permit, which expires on December 15, and will the weather cooperate?” said Kondrashkin.

Recent findings suggest that the fall season on Everest usually lasts until the end of November, since December 1 marks the start of Nepal’s winter climbing season. However, the permit dates may have been extended for this team, which is climbing off the normal route.

Once winter settles in, it will be the turn of Jost Kobusch of Germany, who will attempt to solo Everest in winter along the same route the Russians are now attempting.

In a recent development, on their third and latest trip up the mountain so far, the team only reached 6,700m before hurricane-force winds up to 130kph forced them down, according to former team member Natalyia Belyankina. Belyankina had to leave the expedition for health reasons but has stayed in touch with the others.
